chief_complaint: lip swelling and breathing difficulty after eating shrimp
hpi_details: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with lip swelling and breathing difficulty after eating shrimp. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: She thinks the shrimp was spoiled or contaminated with a toxic preservative from the restaurant.
concerns: She is worried that her throat will close up completely and she will suffocate before anyone can help her.
expectations: She hopes to get an immediate injection or medicine to bring the swelling down and restore normal breathing.

clinical_knowledge.topic: Shellfish Allergy (Tropomyosin, IgE-mediated) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Shellfish Allergy (Tropomyosin, IgE-mediated) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Breathing difficulty after shellfish ingestion requires immediate intramuscular epinephrine and emergency evaluation; long-term management includes shellfish avoidance and an epinephrine auto-injector.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: lip swelling and breathing difficulty after eating shrimp

Key HPI features: A 38-year-old female presents to the clinic with lip swelling and breathing difficulty after eating shrimp. The patient states the symptoms started recently and have been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Shellfish Allergy.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Shellfish Allergy (Tropomyosin, IgE-mediated).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Scombroid (histamine) fish poisoning without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Breathing difficulty or throat tightness — treat as anaphylaxis.
management_principles: Treat the current reaction with intramuscular epinephrine and emergency evaluation; after recovery, avoid implicated shellfish and prescribe an epinephrine auto-injector
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

teaching.one_liner: An IgE-mediated reaction to tropomyosin in shellfish causing lip swelling, hives, or breathing difficulty shortly after ingestion.
red_flags: Breathing difficulty or throat tightness — treat as anaphylaxis

must_ask.say: What shellfish did you eat, and how soon after did symptoms start?
Did your lips swell, or did you have trouble breathing?
Has this happened before with shellfish?
Does this happen with all shellfish — shrimp, crab, lobster — or just one?
Are you already avoiding shellfish, and do you carry epinephrine?

history.answer: I ate some shrimp about an hour ago, and now my lips are all swollen and I can barely breathe.
It started about an hour ago right after lunch, beginning with lip swelling and then sudden breathing difficulty about 30 minutes later.
I am struggling to catch my breath even while sitting completely still, and my chest feels very tight.
It has been getting continuously worse since it started, with no signs of letting up.
I ate grilled shrimp pasta about an hour ago at lunch. The food tasted normal, and no one else who ate with me became ill.
My lips began tingling and swelling up noticeably within fifteen minutes of eating the shrimp.
My throat feels swollen and tight on the inside, and it feels difficult and uncomfortable to swallow my saliva.
Yes, I can hear a whistling sound from my throat and chest whenever I try to take a breath.
I broke out in intensely itchy red hives across my neck and chest right around the time my breathing became difficult.
I have had a dry cough since my throat tightened up, but I have no phlegm and no fever.
I don't have sharp chest pain, but there is a heavy, tight squeezing feeling across my chest.
No, lying down doesn't make a difference, and this didn't wake me from sleep since it only started an hour ago.
My heart is beating very fast and I feel slightly lightheaded, but I haven't passed out.
No, I have never coughed up any blood.
Eating the shrimp definitely brought this on, and nothing I do makes it feel any better.
No, my legs are not swollen at all, and my weight has been completely stable.
No, neither leg hurts or looks swollen, and I haven't had recent surgery or long flights.
I feel completely drained and weak since this started, but there is no abnormal bleeding or black stools.
My lips feel numb and swollen and I feel terrified because I can't breathe, but my fingers and feet are not tingling.
A few months ago I had mild lip tingling after eating crab, but it went away quickly so I didn't think much of it.
I haven't eaten other shellfish like lobster or squid recently, but I can eat regular white fish without any issues.
I was not actively avoiding shellfish because I did not realize that earlier mild reaction was a true allergy.
I was wondering if the seafood was spoiled or if they used some chemical preservative that reacted badly with me.
I'm terrified that my throat might shut tight and I won't be able to breathe at all.
I'm hoping you can give me a quick shot or medicine right now to open my airways and stop my lips from swelling.
I don't have any chronic medical conditions like asthma, heart problems, or hypertension.
I have never had surgery and have never been admitted to a hospital.
I am not taking any prescription medications, over-the-counter painkillers, aspirin, or supplements.
I have no known allergies to penicillin or any other medications.
I have never smoked cigarettes.
I only drink socially, having a glass of wine once or twice a month.
I work as an office manager indoors, with no exposure to dust, chemicals, birds, or mold.
My mother has seasonal pollen allergies, but nobody in my family has asthma or severe food allergies.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, and my cycles are always regular.
My husband had a vasectomy years ago, so there is no chance I could be pregnant.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 106/68 mmHg, pulse 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, body temperature 36.7°C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air.
The patient is alert but visibly anxious and in moderate respiratory distress, using neck accessory muscles to breathe, with marked swelling of both lips.
Prominent angioedema of the upper and lower lips with mild uvular edema; posterior pharynx is clear without tonsillar exudate.
Normal jugular venous pressure without engorgement or distension.
Mild intercostal retractions visible on inspiration; symmetrical chest expansion with no chest wall tenderness.
Percussion notes are resonant bilaterally across all lung fields.
Diffuse expiratory wheezing heard throughout both lung fields with a prolonged expiratory phase; no crackles or stridor.
Tachycardic regular rhythm with normal S1 and S2; no murmurs, gallops, rubs, or third heart sound.
Multiple raised erythematous urticarial wheals scattered across the anterior neck, upper chest, and arms; no cyanosis.
No pitting edema over either pretibial area or ankle.
Both calves are symmetric without swelling, redness, warmth, or tenderness on palpation.
